c.en: behave politely
ex: Whenever we had guests, she'd remind me to **mind my manners**: stand up when an older person enters and greet them first.
At my friend's wedding I tried hard to **mind my manners** because I didn't know most of the guests.
My grandfather always tells me to **mind my manners** when we visit his old colleagues.
In a job interview, you really have to **mind your manners**, even if the interviewer is very friendly.

c.en: a way of showing you respect someone
ex: People often put their right hand on their heart when they greet someone, which is **a sign of respect**.
In our culture, pouring tea for older people first is **a sign of respect**.
Standing up when the teacher comes into the room is still seen as **a sign of respect**.
Calling your boss by their full name is **a sign of respect** in many companies.

c.en: less strict or formal
ex: I'd say things have become a lot **more relaxed**, especially in big cities.
Young people are much **more relaxed** about dress codes than their parents were.
Our new teacher is **more relaxed** about deadlines, as long as we tell her in advance.
Family dinners in my house are **more relaxed** at the weekend, when nobody is in a hurry.

c.w: on the tip of my tongue
c.en: almost remembered, but not quite
ex: An hour later I'll see someone and the name is **on the tip of my tongue**, but I just can't remember it.
The answer was **on the tip of my tongue** during the exam, but it came back to me only on the bus home.
What's that film with the talking robot called? It's **on the tip of my tongue**.
I knew the word in English, it was right **on the tip of my tongue**, but I had to describe it instead.

c.en: a clever way of doing something
ex: The best **trick** is to use the name straight away, because saying it out loud helps it stick.
My favourite **trick** for learning new words is writing them on sticky notes around my room.
There's a simple **trick** to waking up early: put your alarm on the other side of the room.
My mum taught me a **trick** for remembering phone numbers by splitting them into small groups.

c.en: feel offended by something
ex: Honestly, I don't **take it personally**, because I forget names all the time myself.
If a friend doesn't reply to my message for a day, I try not to **take it personally**.
My teacher's comments were quite harsh, but I knew I shouldn't **take it personally**.
When a customer is rude, a good shop assistant doesn't **take it personally**.

c.en: very clever and quick-thinking
ex: He's eighty, but he's still as **sharp as a tack**.
My little sister is as **sharp as a tack**: she solves maths puzzles faster than I do.
Even after a twelve-hour shift, our manager is always as **sharp as a tack** in meetings.
My grandmother is as **sharp as a tack** and remembers every family birthday.

c.en: feeling and acting younger than your age
ex: He really is **young at heart**.
My grandfather is seventy, but he's **young at heart** and still plays football with us.
Our neighbour is **young at heart**: she learned to ride a bike at sixty.
You can stay **young at heart** if you keep learning new things.

c.en: from the very beginning, with no previous knowledge
ex: I learned Excel almost **from scratch**: formulas, charts and later even some simple automation.
My uncle built his small business **from scratch**, with no help from anyone.
When my laptop crashed, I had to write the whole essay again **from scratch**.
She started learning Korean **from scratch** last year, and now she can watch dramas without subtitles.

c.en: calm and not annoyed with someone
ex: She was always very **patient with** me, even when I asked the same question three times.
A good driving instructor has to be **patient with** nervous students.
My father is very **patient with** my little brother when they do homework together.
Doctors need to be **patient with** elderly people who don't understand medical words.

c.en: finding something very difficult
ex: She was really **struggling with** the maths section, and her practice scores were very low.
At first, I was **struggling with** the listening part because the speakers talked so fast.
Many students are **struggling with** stress before their final exams.
My cousin was **struggling with** his new job, so I helped him with the reports.

c.en: extremely happy
ex: When she called me with the results, she was **over the moon**.
My parents were **over the moon** when I got into university.
I was **over the moon** when my band score went up from 6 to 7.
The whole team was **over the moon** after winning the city championship.

c.en: was remembered for a long time
ex: First of all, he **left a lasting impression** on me.
My first trip to Samarkand **left a lasting impression** on me because of the beautiful old buildings.
The speech our teacher gave on graduation day **left a lasting impression** on all of us.
That documentary about the ocean **left a lasting impression** on me, and now I avoid plastic bags.

c.en: feel angry with yourself for a mistake
ex: I completely forgot to ask for his email address, and I still **kick myself** about it.
I **kick myself** every time I remember that I didn't buy that laptop when it was on sale.
If I don't practise speaking now, I'll **kick myself** after the exam.
I could **kick myself** for missing the last bus by just one minute.

c.en: someone or something everybody knows
ex: In our area, his name is basically **a household name**.
After her song went viral, the young singer became **a household name**.
Some brands, like Coca-Cola, are **a household name** all over the world.
He was an ordinary teacher, but his YouTube lessons made him **a household name** in Uzbekistan.

c.en: people telling each other about something
ex: It's all **word of mouth**: he has never paid for advertising.
Our English centre got most of its students through **word of mouth**.
The best restaurants in my city don't advertise; they rely on **word of mouth**.
I found my tutor by **word of mouth**, because a friend recommended her.

c.en: differences between older and younger people
ex: Shared interests are one of the best ways to bridge **the generation gap**.
Technology has made **the generation gap** much wider, because my grandparents hardly use smartphones.
Music is a good example of **the generation gap**: my dad can't stand the songs I listen to.
Cooking together with my grandmother helps us close **the generation gap**.

c.en: someone who keeps learning all their life
ex: In today's world, being **a lifelong learner** is almost a requirement.
My grandfather is **a lifelong learner**: at seventy he started learning English online.
Good teachers are usually **lifelong learners** themselves.
I want to be **a lifelong learner**, not someone who stops reading after university.

c.en: learning by trying and making mistakes
ex: After that, it's mostly **trial and error**: you start small, make mistakes and adjust.
I learned to cook mainly through **trial and error**, and my family ate a lot of burnt rice.
Finding the best way to prepare for IELTS was a process of **trial and error**.
Most small businesses grow by **trial and error** rather than by following a perfect plan.

c.en: do their fair share of the work
ex: Everyone in a family should **pull their weight**, not just the mother.
In group projects, there's always someone who doesn't **pull their weight**.
If every flatmate **pulls their weight**, the flat stays clean without any arguments.
Our coach says the team only wins when all the players **pull their weight**.

c.en: show others how to behave by doing it yourself
ex: In other words, parents need to **lead by example**.
A good manager should **lead by example** and arrive at work on time.
If teachers want students to read more, they should **lead by example** and talk about the books they read.
My older brother always **leads by example**: he started exercising, and soon we all joined him.

c.en: like each other immediately
ex: Shared interests give you something to talk about, and that's often how people **hit it off**.
My best friend and I **hit it off** on the first day of school because we both loved football.
I was nervous about meeting my new roommate, but we **hit it off** straight away.
They **hit it off** at a friend's party and have been inseparable ever since.

c.en: help someone show their best qualities
ex: The best teachers know how to **bring out the best in** each student.
Competition can **bring out the best in** athletes, but it can also create a lot of stress.
My best friend always **brings out the best in** me; I'm more confident when she's around.
Difficult situations sometimes **bring out the best in** people.

c.en: someone who enjoys being with and talking to people
ex: Someone who is **a people person** is often more popular than the smartest person in the office.
My sister is **a people person**, so working as a hotel receptionist is perfect for her.
I'm not really **a people person**; I prefer working quietly on my own.
To be a good tour guide, you need to be **a people person**.
